name: Jamal Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing electrical engineering in Sheffield, and I share a flat with two lads from my course, Dev and Callum. Mornings are lectures in circuits and maths, afternoons are lab sheets, and Thursday evenings I go to the engineering society's pub quiz. I do all my notes by hand in a green notebook my gran gave me, and everyone else laughs because they paste things into chatbots. My gran sold a flat to set up a fund for my fees, so money's not what keeps me up. What keeps me up is whether the jobs will be there when I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly, because Dev would never let it go. Half my course has been telling me I'm behind for refusing chatbots, so I'd enjoy that a bit. Mostly I'd say the maths still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel a little relieved, but only a little. Graduate schemes for engineers are getting smaller every year, even before any of this. The firms will still squeeze entry pay and call it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. I'd keep doing circuit problems by hand and join the placement group the student union runs, because I want a summer placement at the water utility. I'd also email three firms in my second year instead of waiting for the careers fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, because it's the world I planned for. A bit flat too, because the argument with my flatmate Dev about chatbots would just stop and I kind of like that argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the squeeze on entry pay stays. Who worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said the squeeze on entry pay stays. Who worries you most? My cousin Ayesha applied to 60 places for a civil engineering job and got two interviews. That was before anyone said the word AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your gran say about you never touching the chatbots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would your gran say about you never touching the chatbots? She'd laugh and say I'm as stubborn as my grandad. Then she'd tell me to try a tool once it's proven, and I'd say fair, but proven by whom and owned by whom?

say: I'd say the hype was overblown and the **maths** still matters.
I'd tell Dev (my flatmate) he can keep his chatbot, I'll keep my notebook.
think: I feel **a little relieved**, but I still expect small graduate schemes.
Firms will keep **squeezing entry pay** and call it efficiency.
do: Keep doing circuit problems **by hand** in my green notebook.
Join the student union's **placement group** and email three firms early.
Aim for a summer placement at the **water utility**.
feel: **Calm**, but a little flat because the chatbot argument would end.
S0.quote: Graduate schemes for engineers are getting smaller every year, even before any of this.
fieldNote: His stubbornness about chatbots is partly pride and partly distrust of who owns the tools.
His worry is the shrinking **graduate scheme**, not AI itself.
Gran's fund means money is safe; the job market is the stress.

steps.text: Keep working circuit problems by hand in the green notebook
Email three firms about placements before the careers fair
Join the student union placement group and go to its meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being sold to us as a gift when it's really a cost cut. At the placement group I'd ask who decides which jobs shrink and who pays for retraining. I'd say it online too, though I mostly lurk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking tasks it takes are exactly the junior ones I'd do: checking drawings, writing reports, coding a test script. If firms hire fewer juniors, my cohort of about 150 is competing for fewer seats. I don't like saying it, but I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my second-year project towards the hands-on side, like power systems and the substations my uncle Raj works on. I'd also go to the union-backed careers talk and ask the awkward questions. And I'd maybe, finally, try a chatbot once, to know what I'm arguing against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry. I don't think the change is the problem, I think the speed with nobody in charge is. I feel it in my stomach when a lecturer says 'many of you will supervise software rather than write it'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try a chatbot once. What would make that okay for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd try a chatbot once. What would make that okay for you? If the course made it part of an assessed lab so everyone was on the same footing and the data stayed in the university. I don't want to hand my work to a company for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in your family? My mum teaches maths and her school's already got an AI marking trial. She says it's fine, but she goes quiet when I ask if her job is safe.

say: I'd say it's a **cost cut** sold as a gift.
I'd ask at the placement group who decides which jobs shrink.
think: Junior tasks like **checking drawings** and test scripts are the ones I'd do.
With about 150 on my course, **fewer junior seats** worries me.
do: Push my second-year project towards **power systems** and substations.
Ask awkward questions at the union-backed **careers talk**.
Try a chatbot **once**, only inside a university lab.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit angry about the speed with nobody in charge.
S1.quote: I don't think the change is the problem, I think the speed with nobody in charge is.
fieldNote: He accepts a tool only on fair terms: shared footing and data kept inside the university.
Moves from a **principled stance** to a cautious experiment.
His mum's marking trial shows the fear sits close to home.

steps.text: Choose a power systems project for the second-year module
Ask careers speakers which junior roles are being cut
Try one chatbot task inside a supervised university lab

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules now: public ownership of the biggest systems, a pause on firing people, a basic income. Nobody voted for this speed. I'd probably say it at a protest, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my degree could be worthless before I finish the second year. I'd graduate into a world where my whole course is a robot's job. That is the part I can't say in the society pub quiz without crying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at university, because leaving gains nothing. I'd join the student union's campaign and go to the first march, and I'd ask my gran to keep the fund untouched. I'd also try to learn how the grid works, because power and wiring still need hands for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have trouble sleeping, and I'd check the news at three in the morning on my phone, which I do now about exams anyway. And angry, because I picked this course for stability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you change course? I'd think about it every night but I wouldn't know what to change to, since AGI does the thinking in every subject. Maybe a trade, maybe nursing. My flatmate Callum says that's panic and he might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night? I'd say I'm sorry for making you and Dad pay for a degree that might not pay back. And she'd say it's not your fault, and then we'd both be crying on the phone.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules**: public ownership, no mass firings, a basic income.
I'd say nobody voted for this **speed**.
think: My degree could be worth **nothing** before I even finish.
I'd be **scared** for my family, not only for myself.
do: Stay at university and join the student union's **campaign** and first march.
Ask Gran to leave the **fund untouched** for now.
Learn how the **power grid** works, since wiring needs hands longer.
feel: **Alarmed**, sleepless, and angry that I chose this course for stability.
S2.quote: I'd graduate into a world where my whole course is a robot's job.
fieldNote: His progressive politics turn into **collective action**: protest, union, public ownership.
Distress shows when he talks about his mum and the family fund.
Flatmate Callum calls his change-course thought panic; he half agrees.

steps.text: Go to the student union march against mass firings
Write to my MP about a basic income
Ask Gran to keep the education fund untouched
Sit in on the second-year power grid lectures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's enough to demand rules if everyone pushes now. I'd say it to my union group first and then to my uncle Raj, who thinks I'm being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I have a window. I'd finish the degree around 2030, so it lands right as I qualify. Five years is a window, but a window is not a plan, and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my first year and join the student union properly. In second year I'd pick substation and grid modules, and spend summers on site with Uncle Raj. I'd also stop the stubborn thing and learn two AI tools, so I can argue from inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to breathe. Five years feels like a long exam period, scary but with a plan. I'd probably still wake up some nights thinking about the 2031 date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn two AI tools. Is that a change of heart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd learn two AI tools. Is that a change of heart? Not really a change of heart, more like deciding it's better to know the tool than be told what it does. I'd still keep the notebook for my own thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the university in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the university in those five years? Honest advice on which jobs are going and a way to switch course without losing the fees. Right now they only say 'lifelong learning' and that tells me nothing.

say: I'd say five years is enough time to **demand rules** if everyone pushes.
I'd tell Uncle Raj (his uncle) this isn't being dramatic.
think: I'd see a **window**, but a window isn't a plan.
I'd graduate around 2030, so it lands **right as I qualify**.
do: Join the student union properly and take **grid modules** in second year.
Spend summers on site with Uncle Raj, a **substation engineer**.
Learn **two AI tools** so I can argue from inside.
feel: **Anxious** but able to breathe, like a long exam period.
S3.quote: Five years is a window, but a window is not a plan, and I'd know it.
fieldNote: Five years gives him room to move from **resistance** to informed use.
Wants honest advice and flexible course switching from the university.
Keeps the notebook for private thinking, a boundary he'll hold.

steps.text: Take the substation and grid modules in second year
Work summers on site with my uncle Raj
Learn two AI tools while still handwriting my notes
Attend student union meetings every fortnight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to fix this properly if we vote for it. I'd say we should build retraining and public support while there's no panic. That's the version of me that's allowed to be hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'd have a full career's first stretch before things get strange. I'd finish at 22, work for several years, and have time to change direction. It feels almost fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, aim for a good graduate scheme, and save from the first pay cheque. I'd keep my union membership going and probably learn some AI tools at work when the firm requires it. And I'd stay close to the hands-on side of the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a low hum of worry. I can plan around ten years. What I can't plan around is whether people in charge will do anything with that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if nothing is done in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you blame if nothing is done in those ten years? I'd blame governments and lobbying companies more than the machines, because the machines don't choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old starting engineering then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old starting engineering then? I'd tell them to learn the physics deeply, join a union, and not trust any tool they can't explain. And to do something with their hands.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to build **retraining** and public support.
I'd say we should vote for it before any panic.
think: I'd have the **first stretch** of a career before things get strange.
The hard part is whether **people in charge** use the time.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **graduate scheme** on the grid side.
Save from my first pay cheque and keep **union membership** going.
Learn AI tools at work **when the firm requires** it.
feel: **Calm** with a low hum of worry about who is in charge.
S4.quote: I'd blame governments and lobbying companies more than the machines, because the machines don't choose.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his anger towards **governments and lobbyists** rather than the technology.
He sees time as only useful if institutions act.
Hope here is conditional, not relaxed.

steps.text: Apply to graduate schemes at the grid operator in final year
Put part of every first pay cheque into savings
Keep paying into my union membership

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough for anything to be done, and I'd be in second year with a degree built for a world that's vanished. What would help is public rules in place before it happens, honest careers advice, and a way to switch course without losing the fees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe one thing. People assume I avoid chatbots because I'm afraid of them, but it's because I don't trust who owns them. If someone could show me tools that belong to the public, I'd use them tomorrow.

headlineQuote: People assume I avoid chatbots because I'm afraid of them, but it's because I don't trust who owns them.
portrait: Jamal is an 18-year-old **electrical engineering** student in Sheffield who writes notes by hand and never uses chatbots.
His gran's fund covers fees, so **money is safe**; the job market is what worries him.
He is progressive and union-minded: he blames **companies and governments**, not the machines.
In a fast AGI he turns to **protest and public ownership**, while a slower one lets him learn the tools carefully.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most: his degree could be worthless before he finishes.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **public rules** in place first, honest careers advice and course switching without losing fees.
